title: Advanced Subclinical Atherosclerosis in Young Individuals and Risk of Mortality Over 30 Years: The Coronary Artery Calcium Consortium.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring is a well-established tool for predicting cardiovascular risk, but its long-term prognostic value in young adults remains unclear. As early preventive intervention may yield substantial lifetime benefit, understanding long-term implications of elevated CAC in young adults is important for informing prevention strategies.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the long-term risk of all-cause, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and coronary heart disease (CHD) mortality associated with premature advanced subclinical atherosclerosis.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study used the CAC Consortium dataset, a retrospectively assembled cohort of referred individuals with clinically indicated CAC scans. Using multivariable regression models for time-to-event analysis, the association of CAC with all-cause, CVD, and CHD mortality was assessed, adjusting for age, sex, and traditional atherosclerotic CVD risk factors. Cumulative incidence was derived for these outcomes in 5-year increments up to 30 years using a mixed approach involving the Kaplan-Meier method and Weibull modeling. The proportion of deaths attributable to CVD and CHD across CAC groups was evaluated. Four institutions across the US provided patient-level data to assemble the CAC Consortium. Included in the analysis were adults aged 30 to 45 years from the CAC Consortium. They were followed up for a median of 22.6 years. Study data were analyzed from October 2025 to September 2026.
EXPOSURE: Elevated CAC in adults aged 30 to 45 years, specifically CAC score greater than 90%.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Participants were followed up for underlying cause of mortality.
RESULTS: Among 12 847 participants, the mean (SD) age was 40.5 (3.6) years, and 9922 (77.2%) were male; 9262 (72.1%) had CAC score of 0, 1626 (12.7%) had a CAC score between 75% to 90%, and 1703 (13.3%) had a CAC score greater than 90%. In total, there were 624 deaths (149 CVD and 81 CHD). Multivariable adjusted hazard ratios for CAC score greater than 90% vs CAC score of 0 were 1.87 (95% CI, 1.54-2.27), 2.60 (95% CI, 1.77-3.82), and 3.71 (95% CI, 2.24-6.16), for all-cause, CVD, and CHD mortality, respectively. Over 30 years, the group with a CAC score greater than 90% had significantly higher modeled risk of all-cause (12.9% vs 7.5%), CVD (4.5% vs 1.5%), and CHD (3.0% vs 0.6%) mortality, compared with the group with a CAC score of 0.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Results of this cohort study suggest that young adults with a CAC score greater than 90% face significantly higher long-term risk of all-cause, CVD, and CHD mortality, suggesting potential implications for guiding the intensification of preventive intervention in this high-risk phenotype.

score.why_it_matters: Provides compelling 30-year prognostic data demonstrating that young adults aged 30 to 45 with advanced subclinical atherosclerosis face a nearly fourfold increased risk of coronary heart disease death.
score.bottom_line: In young adults aged 30 to 45 years, a coronary artery calcium score above the 90th percentile is associated with markedly elevated 30-year cardiovascular and all-cause mortality compared to a score of zero. When identified, this premature high-calcium phenotype warrants aggressive, early initiation of cardiovascular preventive therapies.

title: Global Heart Failure Burden Increased Between 1990 and 2023.

score.why_it_matters: Provides updated longitudinal epidemiological data demonstrating the escalating worldwide public health and healthcare burden of heart failure.
score.bottom_line: The global burden of heart failure increased substantially between 1990 and 2023, highlighting the growing demand for preventative measures and heart failure management infrastructure globally.

title: Pacing Related Conduction Delay as an Indicator of Intramural Site of Origin of Focal Ventricular Arrhythmias.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The diagnosis of intramural focal ventricular arrhythmias (VA) can be challenging and is often made in retrospect after a long ineffective procedure.
OBJECTIVES: In this cohort of patients, we aim to assess the value of pace-mapping (PM), stimulus-QRS interval (S-QRS interval), and electrogram (EGM)-QRS intervals to identify the site of origin (SOO) of focal VAs.
METHODS: In a consecutive series of 46 patients with frequent premature ventricular complexes (PVCs), activation mapping and PM were performed to identify VA target sites. VA target sites were defined as sites with matching PM (≥10/12 leads) and/or sites with the earliest activation time. S-QRS interval and bipolar activation time at target sites were assessed and correlated with acute outcomes. If ablation at a target site failed, alternative sites were sought in adjacent anatomical structures. An intramural origin was defined as a VA with early activation time without a matching PM.
RESULTS: Matching PMs were identified for 32 VAs in 30 of the 46 patients. Receiver operating characteristic analysis was performed at the target site/PVC level and demonstrated that a mismatch between S-QRS and EGM-QRS of >26 milliseconds distinguished effective from ineffective ablation sites with a matching PM (area under the curve: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.94-1; sensitivity: 100%; specificity: 88.9%). A mismatch was present in 9 patients, and radiofrequency ablation failed in 8/9 of them. Alternate sites with early activation times (-48.4 ± 37.39 milliseconds) without matching PM, where radiofrequency eliminated the PVCs, were identified in 5/8 patients.
CONCLUSIONS: Conduction delay with matching PMs but late activation indicates a deeper SOO. A cutoff value of >26 milliseconds between S-QRS and EGM-QRS intervals identified deeper-seated VA target sites. This required further mapping to identify alternative ablation sites. A matching PM may not always be indicative of the SOO in patients with PVCs.

score.why_it_matters: Identifies an electrophysiological marker to recognize intramural PVC origins early, avoiding futile ablation at superficial pace-matched sites.
score.bottom_line: A discrepancy between stimulus-QRS and local EGM-QRS intervals (>26 ms) despite a matching pace-map reliably identifies an intramural site of origin where standard ablation will likely fail. Operators should recognize this mismatch to promptly seek alternative ablation targets in adjacent anatomical structures.

title: Embolic Myocardial Infarction From Delayed Left Bundle Lead Perforation.

score.why_it_matters: Highlights a rare and severe thromboembolic complication of left bundle branch pacing resulting from delayed lead perforation into the left ventricular cavity.
score.bottom_line: Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for lead perforation and left-sided thromboembolism when patients with conduction system pacing present with new ischemic events.

title: Don't Blink!-Time for "Instant" PFA?

score.why_it_matters: Provides expert commentary on the evolving efficiency and procedural speed of pulsed field ablation for atrial fibrillation.
score.bottom_line: As an editorial commentary, this article discusses emerging ultra-rapid pulsed field ablation techniques without presenting novel primary data.

title: Safety and Outcomes of Transvenous Lead Extraction of Advisory ePTFE-Coated Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator Leads: A Multicenter Experience With RELIANCE G.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE)-coated implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) leads are associated with progressive coil calcification and rising shock impedance, prompting a recent safety advisory. However, data regarding the safety and efficacy of transvenous lead extraction (TLE) for these chronic leads remain limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the safety, efficacy, and procedural outcomes of TLE in patients with advisory ePTFE-coated ICD leads.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective multicenter study at 13 centers of patients undergoing TLE of ePTFE-coated ICD leads. Primary endpoints included procedural success, complications, and short-term mortality. Multivariable analyses identified predictors of outcomes.
RESULTS: Among 423 patients undergoing extraction of advisory RELIANCE ICD leads (Boston Scientific), mean lead dwell time was 7.5 ± 5.3 years, and impedance-defined coil calcification was present in 15.1%. Laser sheaths were used in 63.8% of procedures and multiple extraction tools in 21.7%. Complete lead removal was achieved in 95.5%, clinical success in 98.8%, and extraction failed occurred in 1.2%. Major complications occurred in 0.9% of patients, with no procedural deaths. Calcified leads were associated with longer dwell times but not higher rates of major complications. Thirty-day mortality was 2.8%, primarily among patients undergoing extraction for infection.
CONCLUSIONS: In this large multicenter cohort, TLE of advisory ePTFE-coated ICD leads was associated with high procedural success and low major complication rates despite long lead dwell times. Outcomes were consistent with contemporary TLE experience and do not suggest increased procedural risk attributable to this lead model. The presence of impedance-defined coil calcification did not adversely affect procedural outcomes, supporting TLE at experienced centers when clinically indicated.

score.why_it_matters: Provides reassuring multicenter safety and efficacy data for extracting advisory ePTFE-coated (Reliance) ICD leads, even in the presence of coil calcification.
score.bottom_line: Transvenous extraction of advisory ePTFE-coated ICD leads at experienced centers carries high clinical success (98.8%) and low major complication rates (0.9%). Impedance-defined coil calcification prolonged dwell time but did not increase procedural risk.

title: The Vein of Marshall Promotes Re-Entry After Pulmonary Vein Reconnection.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postablation re-entrant atrial tachycardia recurrence remains a major limitation of atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation. Pulmonary vein (PV) reconnection and epicardial connections from the left atrium (LA) to the vein of Marshall (VoM) and coronary sinus (CS) in proximity to mitral valve are important contributors. We hypothesized that VoM facilitates arrhythmia induction through interaction with the epicardial region encircled by wide antral circumferential ablation (WACA).
OBJECTIVES: The objective of this study was to systematically evaluate the combined effect of PV reconnection and epicardial VoM connectivity on the occurrence of sustained postablation re-entrant atrial tachycardia using in silico models.
METHODS: Bilayer biatrial models were constructed from electroanatomical and computed tomographic data of 10 patients with AF. Post-AF electrical remodeling and substrate remodeling following the low voltage area distribution, and left-sided WACA were incorporated. Segments of WACA lesions were sequentially restored to simulate PV reconnection. Three connectivity scenarios were evaluated: intact CS-VoM-LA epicardial connection, CS-LA connection only, and no epicardial connections. Sustained re-entry (>10 seconds) was the primary endpoint, and connectivity conditions were compared using patient-level paired vulnerability. Induction of any arrhythmia, tachycardia cycle length, and stable rotor number were secondary outcomes.
RESULTS: Sustained re-entry occurred at 92 of 294 (31.3%) reconnection sites with intact CS-VoM-LA connectivity, 37 of 294 (12.6%) with CS-LA connectivity only, and 29 of 294 (9.9%) without epicardial connectivity. Patient-level paired analysis showed 19.9-percentage-point and 22.7-percentage-point higher vulnerability with intact CS-VoM-LA connectivity compared with CS-LA connectivity alone (95% CI: 7.1-37.3 percentage points) and no epicardial connectivity (95% CI: 7.4-41.3 percentage points), respectively. Mean tachycardia cycle length in the LA was 258.0 ± 25.7 milliseconds, 255.0 ± 31.4 milliseconds, and 251.0 ± 33.9 milliseconds across the 3 scenarios; the average number of stable rotors was 0.6 ± 0.3, 0.7 ± 0.2, and 0.4 ± 0.2, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: The VoM is a critical epicardial driver of arrhythmia after incomplete WACA, underscoring the importance of its targeted ablation.

score.why_it_matters: This computational modeling study provides mechanistic insight into how the vein of Marshall serves as an epicardial bypass facilitating recurrent re-entry after pulmonary vein reconnection.
score.bottom_line: In silico biatrial models demonstrate that an intact vein of Marshall significantly increases vulnerability to sustained re-entrant atrial tachycardia following incomplete pulmonary vein isolation. While supporting vein of Marshall ethanol infusion in persistent AF strategies, clinical validation remains necessary.

title: Pulsed Field Ablation of the Left Atrial Appendage Before Mechanical Closure to Reduce Peri-Device Leak (STUN-AF).
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Left atrial appendage (LAA) closure (LAAC) is plagued by late peri-device leak. We posited that appendage contraction prevents full LAA seal, so conversely, LAA stunning with pulsed field ablation (PFA) of the LAA (left atrial appendage ablation [LAAA]) might promote rapid appendage thrombosis/obliteration.
OBJECTIVES: This study aims to assess the impact of LAAA during concomitant procedures on eliminating leaks.
METHODS: At 3 centers, consecutive patients undergoing concomitant PFA and LAAC also underwent LAAA or did not undergo LAAA, at operator discretion. Initial (∼3-4 months) (29% transesophageal echocardiography/71% computed tomography) and 12-month imaging were compared with a primary composite outcome of LAA patency, defined as either detectable flow into the LAA or evidence of echo-free space/contrast medium behind the device.
RESULTS: Among 317 total patients undergoing PFA and LAAC, including 222 patients who underwent LAAA and 95 who did not (control patients), all underwent initial imaging and 126 reached 12-month imaging follow-up. Device compression was 28% with LAAA vs 25% without LAAA (P < 0.001). Implantation success was 100%. The periprocedural adverse event rate was 2% in both groups. The primary composite outcome of LAA patency was significantly reduced with LAAA vs no-LAAA, both at 3-4 months (29% vs 64%; P < 0.001) and at 12 months (4% vs 42%; P < 0.001). Device-related thrombus rates were low and similar (2.3% vs 3.2%; P = 0.7). A validation subset including only patients with alternating LAAA assignment (LAAA: n = 59; no-LAAA: n = 63) again revealed that LAAA was associated with reduced LAA patency (3-4 months: 34% vs 51%; P = 0.06; 12 months: 8% vs 36%; P = 0.2). Final LAA e' velocity was significantly different between groups (17 ± 7 vs 34 ± 16 cm/s; P < 0.001), with higher velocity associated with LAA patency (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: PFA of the LAA has potential to reduce LAA patency during device-based LAAC.

score.why_it_matters: Peri-device leak remains a common limitation of mechanical LAA closure; this study introduces a novel concept of stunning the appendage with pulsed field ablation prior to device deployment to significantly improve seal rates.
score.bottom_line: In patients undergoing concomitant PFA and LAAC, intentional pulsed field ablation of the LAA before device implantation was safe and associated with a marked reduction in LAA patency at 12 months (4% vs 42%). While promising, randomized trials are required before this technique can be integrated into standard practice.

title: Bromocriptine for Myocardial Recovery in Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: Design and Rationale of the REBIRTH Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: There is evidence suggesting that bromocriptine potentially improves outcomes among women with peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM); however, there is currently no randomized controlled trial comparing bromocriptine vs placebo on top of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in a diverse, multiethnic cohort in North America.
OBJECTIVES: The REBIRTH trial will enroll 200 women with PPCM to evaluate whether the addition of oral bromocriptine to GDMT is superior to placebo for improving myocardial function and event-free survival. In addition to the randomized trial, REBIRTH will enroll 50 women with PPCM excluded from randomization because of breastfeeding into an observational cohort.
METHODS: The principal inclusion criteria are ≥18 years of age, within 5-months postpartum, and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40%. The primary endpoint is LVEF at 6 months postrandomization. Secondary endpoints include LVEF at 12 months, survival free from major events (ie, death, heart transplantation, or implantation of a durable left ventricular assist device), and survival free from heart failure hospitalization for up to 3 years.
RESULTS: The study is currently enrolling women in both the randomized trial and observational breastfeeding cohort. Primary results are expected to be reported in 2027.
CONCLUSIONS: REBIRTH will determine whether the addition of bromocriptine to GDMT for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction improves postpartum myocardial recovery and clinical outcomes in a diverse cohort of women with PPCM. (Randomized Evaluation of Bromocriptine in Myocardial Recovery Therapy for PPCM [REBIRTH]; NCT05180773).

score.why_it_matters: The REBIRTH trial addresses a major evidence gap regarding whether bromocriptine on top of standard heart failure therapy improves myocardial recovery and clinical outcomes in North American patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy.
score.bottom_line: This paper outlines the rationale and design of the ongoing REBIRTH randomized trial (NCT05180773), which is evaluating bromocriptine versus placebo in 200 women with PPCM; results are expected in 2027.

title: A REBIRTH of Disease-Specific Therapy: Will Targeting Prolactin Reshape Treatment of Peripartum Cardiomyopathy?

title: Coronary revascularisation in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation: from anatomy to physiology guidance?

score.bottom_line: This review discusses the transition from anatomy- to physiology-guided coronary revascularization in patients undergoing TAVI, highlighting recent clinical trial data and physiological nuances in severe aortic stenosis.

title: Reproducible haemodynamics, unresolved indication: where does thrombectomy for acute pulmonary embolism stand?

score.why_it_matters: Catheter-directed mechanical thrombectomy rapidly restores right ventricular hemodynamics in acute pulmonary embolism, but definitive evidence of improved clinical outcomes is still awaited.
score.bottom_line: Mechanical thrombectomy reliably reverses pulmonary hemodynamic strain in acute PE, though clear clinical indications and superiority over standard therapies remain unresolved pending ongoing randomized trials.

title: Prolonged inflation instead of a double tap: pursuing the optimal deployment strategy for the SAPIEN 3 Ultra RESILIA.

score.bottom_line: This technical commentary evaluates deployment mechanics for the SAPIEN 3 Ultra RESILIA valve, discussing the merits of sustained balloon inflation over repeated expansions.

title: Safety and effectiveness of the Vertex Pulmonary Embolectomy System in acute intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism: the SPIRARE II pivotal trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Percutaneous aspiration thrombectomy can rapidly reduce afterload in acute pulmonary embolism (PE), but catheter stiffness and instability may limit access and prevent effective right ventricle (RV) unloading. The Vertex Pulmonary Embolectomy System with Transforming Fixation (TFX) technology is designed to address current limitations of existing catheter-based systems by separating the flexibility necessary for safe navigation from the support that is essential for procedural control.
AIMS: We aimed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the Vertex Pulmonary Embolectomy System for mechanical aspiration thrombectomy in acute intermediate-risk PE.
METHODS: SPIRARE II was a prospective, single-arm, multicentre pivotal investigation conducted at 19 sites in the United States and Europe. Eligible patients had acute PE (≤14 days), a computed tomography angiography-assessed RV to left ventricle (RV/LV) ratio>0.9, and haemodynamic stability (systolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg). Co-primary endpoints were composite major adverse events (MAE) within 48 hours and core laboratory-assessed RV/LV change from baseline to 48 hours. Prespecified secondary endpoints were collected immediately pre- and post-procedure in all patients including mean pulmonary artery pressure, total pulmonary vascular resistance, and cardiac index.
RESULTS: In 123 patients, the 48-hour composite MAE rate was 2.4% (3/123), meeting the prespecified performance goal (one-sided p<0.0001). The mean RV/LV diameter ratio decreased from 1.44±0.33 at baseline to 1.05±0.21 at 48 hours, a mean reduction of 0.39±0.33, exceeding the prespecified performance goal (p<0.0001).
CONCLUSIONS: The Vertex Pulmonary Embolectomy System met its prespecified safety and effectiveness endpoints in acute intermediate-risk PE. TFX delivered precise, stable control with reliable vessel access, enabling consistent right ventricular unloading. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06576427).

score.why_it_matters: Provides prospective pivotal trial data supporting the safety and acute RV-unloading efficacy of a novel mechanical aspiration thrombectomy system in intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism.
score.bottom_line: In the single-arm SPIRARE II study, the Vertex Pulmonary Embolectomy System achieved significant RV/LV ratio reduction with a low 48-hour major adverse event rate (2.4%), meeting its prespecified performance goals. However, randomized comparative outcomes against standard anticoagulation or other catheter-directed therapies remain needed.

title: Life expectancy after aortic valve replacement: a nationwide analysis.

score.why_it_matters: Provides nationwide real-world benchmark data on post-procedural survival and life expectancy following aortic valve replacement, essential for lifetime management strategies and patient counseling.
score.bottom_line: This nationwide analysis offers updated life-expectancy benchmarks after aortic valve replacement to help guide clinical decision-making and patient expectations.

title: Early outcomes of transcatheter vacuum-assisted mass extraction in the left heart and the aortic arch.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transcatheter vacuum-assisted mass extraction (TVME) in the systemic circulation is increasingly being reported. However, its feasibility, effectiveness, and safety remain poorly defined.
AIMS: We sought to investigate the feasibility, effectiveness and safety of TVME in the left heart and aortic arch.
METHODS: Consecutive patients from 6 centres in the United States and Canada were included. Feasibility was defined as technically successful mass extraction without unplanned cardiac surgery or intraprocedural mortality. The effectiveness endpoint was feasibility with successful debulking of ≥70% mass volume. The primary safety endpoint was the 30-day composite of procedure-attributable mortality, major cardiac structural complications, major vascular complications, Type 3-4 bleeding, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and stroke, all according to Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC)-3 definitions. Intraprocedural events were also reported.
RESULTS: A total of 62 consecutive patients were evaluated. Feasibility was reached in 85.5% of patients and effectiveness in 77.4% of patients - except for 11.3% with suboptimal debulking, 3.2% with access-related case abortion, and 8.1% with case cancellation where no mass was found intraprocedurally. The primary safety endpoint occurred in 14.5% of patients, with a procedure-attributable mortality rate of 3.2%. VARC-3 major cardiac structural complications, major vascular complications, Type 3-4 bleeding, ACS, and stroke occurred in 3.2%, 8.1%, 3.2%, 3.2%, and 6.5% of patients, respectively. Intraprocedural events included hypoxia (6.5%), hypotension (9.7%), embolism (3.2%), air embolism (1.6%), and increased mitral regurgitation (6.5%).
CONCLUSIONS: TVME in left-sided and aortic arch masses is feasible and demonstrates reasonable effectiveness. However, the considerable rate of safety-related events highlights the need for better case selection and procedural refinement, such as optimal embolic protection.

score.why_it_matters: Provides early multicenter safety and effectiveness data on using transcatheter vacuum-assisted extraction for high-risk left-sided intracardiac and aortic arch masses.
score.bottom_line: Transcatheter vacuum-assisted mass extraction in the systemic circulation achieved successful debulking in 77.4% of patients but carried a 14.5% 30-day major complication rate, including a 6.5% stroke risk. Careful patient selection and routine cerebral embolic protection are essential when considering this off-label approach.

title: Coronary artery disease management in patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The optimal management of coronary artery disease in patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) remains uncertain.
AIMS: We aimed to compare clinical outcomes between routine coronary revascularisation and conservative management in patients undergoing TAVI and to assess the relative effectiveness of individual revascularisation strategies by performing a meta-analysis of randomised trials.
METHODS: We conducted a pairwise meta-analysis comparing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with conservative treatment and a network meta-analysis comparing the relative effectiveness of individual strategies, including angiography-guided and physiology-guided PCI. The primary outcome was a study-defined composite endpoint of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Secondary endpoints included the individual outcomes of all-cause death, cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, unplanned revascularisation, and major bleeding.
RESULTS: Five trials (N=1,644 patients) were included in the systematic review, and four were included in the primary quantitative synthesis (N=1,476). Compared with conservative treatment, routine PCI was associated with lower risks of MACE (risk ratio [RR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.65-0.98) and unplanned revascularisation (RR 0.30, 95% CI: 0.11-0.83) and an increased risk of major bleeding (RR 1.57, 95% CI: 1.07-2.32). In the network meta-analysis, physiology-guided PCI significantly reduced MACE, stroke, and unplanned revascularisation compared with conservative treatment and ranked highest for all ischaemic outcomes among revascularisation strategies.
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients referred for TAVI, routine revascularisation reduces the risk of ischaemic outcomes compared with conservative treatment. In this setting, physiology-guided PCI may be associated with the most favourable efficacy profile across available strategies. (PROSPERO: CRD420261330194).

score.why_it_matters: Synthesizes recent RCT evidence on revascularization prior to TAVI, supporting physiology-guided PCI as the optimal strategy to reduce ischemic events despite increased bleeding risks.
score.bottom_line: In patients undergoing TAVI with concomitant coronary artery disease, routine revascularization reduces MACE and unplanned interventions compared to conservative management, with physiology-guided PCI showing the most favorable risk-benefit balance.

title: Determining the Optimal Treatment Strategy for Patients With Combined Aortic Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation.

score.why_it_matters: Provides expert commentary on the clinical dilemma of procedural sequencing and selection (surgical vs. transcatheter) in mixed aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation.
score.bottom_line: Managing combined aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation hinges on distinguishing primary from secondary mitral regurgitation and reassessing mitral severity following relief of aortic stenosis.

title: Multidisciplinary Collaboration in the Performance of Aortic Surgery: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
abstract: Intraoperative management of a patient undergoing cardiac surgery requires continuous and independent interventions by multiple healthcare professionals, including surgeons, anesthesiologists, and perfusionists, among others. Although each clinician performs tasks based on their training and accepted techniques, guidelines, and protocols, an action by one member of the team can have immediate consequences for other team members. Aortic surgery adds a level of complexity, with the need for interventions such as single-lung ventilation, systemic cooling (and subsequent rewarming), and myocardial, cerebral, and visceral protection. Much has been made of the utility of the multidisciplinary team. This scientific statement is intended to approach the patient undergoing aortic surgery from 3 different viewpoints: that of the surgeon, the anesthesiologist, and the perfusionist. This scientific statement is not intended to provide an exhaustive summary of approaches to aortic surgery but rather to illustrate the specific concerns that each member of the team may have.

score.why_it_matters: Provides structured expert guidance on intraoperative multidisciplinary coordination between surgeons, anesthesiologists, and perfusionists during complex aortic surgery.
score.bottom_line: Successful management of complex aortic surgery relies on proactive, closed-loop communication among the surgical, anesthesia, and perfusion teams regarding temperature management, neuroprotection, and hemodynamic targets.

title: Another Dimension of Routine TAVR CT-AI-Based Body Composition and Risk Stratification.

score.why_it_matters: Explores how opportunistic AI-driven body composition profiling on routine pre-TAVR CT scans may enhance frailty assessment and procedural risk stratification.
score.bottom_line: AI-derived body composition metrics from pre-TAVR CT provide non-invasive markers of frailty and cachexia, but further prospective validation is needed before integration into routine pre-procedural risk models.

title: Sirolimus-Coated Balloon Angioplasty for Femoropopliteal Artery Disease Without Tissue Loss: A Secondary Analysis of the SirPAD Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether sirolimus-coated balloon angioplasty performs better than uncoated balloon angioplasty among patients with exertional symptoms due to femoropopliteal artery disease remains uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: This study sought to describe 1-year outcomes after sirolimus-coated balloon angioplasty among participants in the SirPAD (Sirolimus-Coated Balloon for Peripheral Artery Disease) trial with femoropopliteal artery disease.
METHODS: In this analysis of the multicenter, randomized, blinded-endpoint SirPAD trial, we evaluated outcomes for patients with femoropopliteal target lesions and without tissue loss (Rutherford category ≤4, Fontaine stage ≤III). A secondary subgroup was restricted to patients with a lower disease burden, excluding ischemic rest pain, prior major amputation, or below-the-knee revascularization. We compared the 1-year rate of: 1) target-lesion revascularization (TLR); 2) the composite of TLR and any unplanned amputation; 3) major adverse limb events; and 4) all-cause death.
RESULTS: Among 597 patients, median age was 71 years, 34.7% were women, and median target-lesion length was 150 mm; 53.8% had total occlusion. After 1 year, 50 patients (17.0%) had undergone TLR in the sirolimus-coated balloon group vs 82 (27.1%) among control subjects (absolute risk difference [ARD]: -10.1%; 95% CI: -16.6 to -3.0). Any amputation or any TLR occurred in 17.7% and 27.1% of patients respectively (ARD: -9.4%; 95% CI: -16.0 to -2.7). Major adverse limb events occurred in 4.1% vs 8.9% of patients, respectively (ARD: -4.8%; 95% CI: -9.0 to -0.8). One-year all-cause death was similar (3.7% vs 5.3%).
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with femoropopliteal artery disease and no tissue loss, sirolimus-coated balloon angioplasty was associated with a lower 1-year rate of TLR compared with uncoated balloon angioplasty. These findings are descriptive rather than confirmatory. (Sirolimus-Coated Balloon for Peripheral Artery Disease; NCT04238546).

score.why_it_matters: Provides randomized evidence supporting sirolimus-coated balloons as an effective non-paclitaxel alternative for reducing target-lesion revascularization in femoropopliteal peripheral artery disease.
score.bottom_line: In patients with femoropopliteal disease without tissue loss, sirolimus-coated balloon angioplasty reduced 1-year target-lesion revascularization and major adverse limb events compared with plain balloon angioplasty. While descriptive, these findings strengthen the clinical utility of 'limus'-based drug delivery in peripheral endovascular interventions.

title: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy Using a Conduction System Pacing Defibrillation Lead in Patients Meeting CRT-D Indications: Six-Month Clinical Outcomes Results From the ASCEND CSP Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Conduction system pacing (CSP) via left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) is a physiologic alternative to conventional biventricular (BiV) pacing for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), but prospective data using purpose-built implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) leads are limited.
OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this study was to evaluate procedural success, defibrillation efficacy, safety, and 6-month clinical outcomes of left bundle branch-optimized cardiac resynchronization therapy (LOT-CRT) delivered with a purpose-built CSP ICD lead and compare outcomes to conventional BiV-CRT.
METHODS: A total of 52 CRT defibrillator patients (age 66 ± 10 years, 31.4% female, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 29.5 ± 6.7%, left bundle branch block [LBBB] 66.7%, QRSd 164.6 ± 25.3 milliseconds, 29.4% ischemic) in the ASCEND CSP IDE (A Stylet-Driven ICD Lead Intended for Conduction System Pacing IDE Study) study underwent attempted implantation of a CSP ICD lead and a coronary sinus lead (LOT-CRT). Implant success, safety and efficacy outcomes, electrocardiographic characteristics, echocardiographic remodeling, heart failure status, patient-reported quality of life, and CRT response were assessed through 6 months. Outcomes were compared with a propensity-matched conventional CRT cohort (BiV-CRT).
RESULTS: Implantation succeeded in 98.1% (51 of 52), with LBBAP capture achieved in all (51 of 51). Freedom from CSP lead-related serious adverse device effects through 6 months was 98.1% (95% CI: 87.1%-99.7%). Defibrillation was successful in all tested patients (100%). Compared with baseline, QRS narrowed by 30.4 ms and LVEF increased by 10.4 points (both P < 0.0001), with a CRT response (≥5%) in 71.1% and super-response (≥14.5%) in 34.2%. Compared with matched BiV-CRT patients from the MORE-CRT MPP (MORE response on Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy with MultiPoint Pacing) study, lead-related events were similar (2.0% vs 2.5%; P = 1.0), LVEF increase was greater (10.4 points vs 4.6 points; P = 0.0005) with more responders (≥5%) and super-responders (≥14.5%) (71.1% vs 48.5%; P = 0.0107 and 34.2% vs 7.8%; P < 0.0001, respectively), and more patients improved by clinical composite score (76.5% vs 52.0%; P = 0.0016). Significant improvements were seen with LOT-CRT in both LBBB and non-LBBB patients.
CONCLUSIONS: LOT-CRT with a dedicated CSP ICD lead achieved high implant success, preserved defibrillation efficacy, and had favorable safety, with greater left ventricular systolic function and clinical improvement than matched conventional CRT, supporting CSP-based CRT defibrillator therapy.

score.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the feasibility, safety, and defibrillation efficacy of a dedicated, purpose-built ICD lead for conduction system pacing in CRT-D candidates.
score.bottom_line: In this prospective IDE cohort of 52 patients, LOT-CRT using a dedicated CSP ICD lead achieved a 98% implant success rate, reliable defibrillation, and superior 6-month echocardiographic remodeling compared to matched biventricular pacing controls. Larger randomized trials are warranted before widespread adoption.

title: Assessment and Reversibility of Hepatic Abnormalities in Heart Failure: Liver in Heart Failure.
abstract: Hepatic abnormalities in non-Fontan heart failure result from congestive hepatopathy and hypoperfusion-related ischemic injury, compounded by neurohormonal activation and systemic inflammation. Assessment of liver disease severity is challenging because standard liver biochemistries, serum fibrosis markers, severity score models, elastography, and imaging modalities have limited diagnostic accuracy in congestive hepatopathy, and hepatic fibrosis is often heterogeneous on histology in this population. Management focuses on optimization of cardiac function through medical therapy or mechanical circulatory support. Although liver biochemical abnormalities frequently improve with restoration of cardiac function, histologic reversibility is variable and not consistently observed. In patients with advanced heart failure needing heart transplantation, histologic cirrhosis and/or fibrosis accompanied by portal hypertension may merit consideration of combined heart-liver transplantation, but correlation between fibrosis and clinical outcomes varies. There remains an unmet need for tests that can reliably assess liver disease severity and predict liver outcomes in non-Fontan congestive hepatopathy.

score.why_it_matters: Synthesizes the diagnostic and prognostic challenges of congestive hepatopathy in advanced heart failure, particularly during evaluation for heart or dual-organ transplantation.
score.bottom_line: Routine liver tests and noninvasive fibrosis markers have limited diagnostic accuracy in non-Fontan congestive hepatopathy, and while biochemical abnormalities often resolve after hemodynamic optimization, histologic reversibility remains inconsistent.

title: Cardiac Structure and Function in Women After Preeclampsia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Preeclampsia increases the risk of long-term heart failure (HF) by 4-fold. Unfortunately, however, universal guidelines for postpartum HF surveillance are lacking. Stage B/subclinical HF has been shown to predict risk of major adverse cardiac outcomes. Some suggest that initiating cardioprotective therapy at this early stage can reduce progression to symptomatic HF.
OBJECTIVES: The aim of this review was to explore cardiac structure and function in women with a history of preeclampsia and to identify when subclinical HF develops in this group.
METHODS: A systematic search of MEDLINE, EMBASE and CINAHL was conducted according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines to identify all studies assessing left ventricular function on transthoracic echocardiography in women with a history of preeclampsia.
RESULTS: A total of 45 case-control studies comprising 8,991 women, including 2,288 women with a history of preeclampsia, were included in the final analysis. During pregnancy, women with preeclampsia had a higher left ventricular mass index (LVMI) (standard mean difference: 10.85 [95% CI: 6.30-15.39]), relative wall thickness (0.05 [95% CI: 0.03-0.08]), E/e' (1.58 [95% CI: 1.02-2.13]), isovolumetric relaxation time (8.74 [95% CI: 3.14-14.34]), lower E/A ratio (-0.27 [95% CI: -0.51 to -0.04]) and reduced absolute global longitudinal strain (GLS) values (2.27 [95% CI: 0.43-4.11]), indicating reduced myocardial function compared with normotensive controls. Postpartum, GLS remained reduced, and LVMI remained elevated in women with a history of preeclampsia. This difference persisted out to 10 years postpartum. There was no significant difference in all other variables >6 months postpartum. Evidence for persistent LVMI elevation >6 months postpartum was not robust in sensitivity analyses excluding overlapping cohorts. Left ventricular ejection fraction and right ventricular function remained similar in the preeclampsia and control groups throughout.
CONCLUSIONS: Preeclampsia is associated with subclinical myocardial dysfunction, characterized by impaired GLS and increased LVMI. Persistent impairment in GLS was observed up to 10 years postpartum, whereas the association with elevated LVMI beyond 6 months postpartum should be interpreted with caution. Further studies are required to assess when subclinical myocardial dysfunction progresses to symptomatic clinical HF.

score.why_it_matters: Identifies that preeclampsia is associated with persistent subclinical left ventricular systolic dysfunction (impaired GLS) lasting up to a decade postpartum despite normal conventional ejection fraction.
score.bottom_line: Subclinical myocardial impairment detected by reduced global longitudinal strain can persist for up to 10 years following preeclampsia, supporting closer long-term cardiovascular monitoring in these women.

title: Three ablation strategies using very high-power short-duration catheter in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation: The Q-INDEX randomized trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Very high-power short-duration (vHPSD; 90 W/4 sec) ablation shortens pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) but produces shallower lesions that may be inadequate in the thick anterior left atrium.
OBJECTIVE: To compare vHPSD, ablation index (AI)-guided, and hybrid strategies for PVI in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
METHODS: In this multicenter, randomized, open-label trial, 150 patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation were assigned 1:1:1 with the QDOT MICRO catheter to (1) AI-guided (AI 500 anterior, 400 elsewhere), (2) hybrid (AI-guided anterior [AI 500], vHPSD elsewhere), or (3) vHPSD (90 W/4 sec, all segments). The primary endpoint was total ablation time; secondary endpoints included acute PV reconnection, safety, and 1-year freedom from atrial arrhythmia.
RESULTS: Acute PVI was achieved in all patients. Total ablation time was longest with AI-guided and shortest with vHPSD ablation (median 2220 vs 1450 vs 794 sec; P < .001). Acute reconnection across the 14 PV segments was lowest with AI-guided and highest with vHPSD (7.7% vs 9.4% vs 10.6%; P = .40). One-year freedom from atrial arrhythmia was 92.0%, 85.4%, and 77.6%, respectively (log-rank P = .13; for AI-guided vs vHPSD; P = .049). No tamponade occurred; steam pops occurred only in the 90 W groups. Two minor periprocedural strokes occurred (both vHPSD; full recovery), and silent cerebral lesions on magnetic resonance imaging did not differ among the groups (5%, 10%, 0%; P = .35).
CONCLUSION: Uniform vHPSD more than halved PVI ablation time but was associated with the lowest 1-year efficacy, whereas the hybrid strategy preserved efficiency without significant loss of durability. These exploratory findings-from a trial powered for ablation time-support region-tailored lesion depth in point-by-point ablation and warrant confirmation.

score.why_it_matters: This randomized trial cautions against uniform very high-power short-duration (vHPSD) ablation across all left atrial segments due to lower 1-year durability compared to standard AI-guided or hybrid strategies.
score.bottom_line: While uniform vHPSD (90 W/4 s) significantly cuts procedural ablation time, it yielded lower 1-year freedom from atrial arrhythmias (77.6% vs 92.0%) compared to AI guidance. A hybrid approach—using AI-guided lesions anteriorly and vHPSD elsewhere—balances procedural efficiency with clinical efficacy.

title: Intact En Bloc Percutaneous Extraction of a Chronically Implanted Aorto-Ostial Right Coronary Artery Stent.

score.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the technical feasibility of percutaneous extraction of a chronically implanted ostial coronary stent in highly exceptional circumstances.
score.bottom_line: This technical case report illustrates a rare bailout retrieval of an aorto-ostial RCA stent, highlighting procedural ingenuity without impacting daily practice.

title: Feasibility and Restenosis Predictors of Optical Frequency Domain Imaging-Guided Drug-Coated Balloon Treatment for Femoropopliteal Lesions.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The clinical utility of optical frequency domain imaging (OFDI) for guiding endovascular therapy in femoropopliteal lesions has not been established. Additionally, the prognostic value of OFDI findings during drug-coated balloon (DCB) treatment for femoropopliteal lesions has never been evaluated.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to clarify the feasibility of OFDI-guided DCB treatment and investigate the OFDI findings associated with restenosis after DCB treatment in femoropopliteal lesions.
METHODS: This multicenter, prospective, observational study included patients with symptomatic, nonseverely calcified femoropopliteal lesions who underwent DCB treatment under OFDI guidance. Procedural success was defined as residual stenosis of less than 30% without flow compromise and without any procedural complications. The primary outcome was restenosis of the target lesion, defined as a peak systolic velocity ratio of ≥2.5, as measured by duplex ultrasound at rest or target lesion revascularization.
RESULTS: A total of 202 lesions were initially enrolled, of which 35 (17.3%) were excluded primarily because of severe calcification or inadequate OFDI data. Among the 167 analyzable lesions included in the present analysis, the procedural success rate and 1-year freedom from restenosis were 91.6% and 85.5%, respectively. In the procedural OFDI findings, a calcified nodule in the target lesion (subdistribution hazard ratio: 3.25; 95% CI: 1.01-10.42; P = 0.048) was associated with restenosis.
CONCLUSIONS: OFDI-guided DCB treatment is feasible in selected femoropopliteal lesions. An OFDI-detected calcified nodule is associated with an increased risk of restenosis after DCB treatment for femoropopliteal lesions.

score.why_it_matters: It demonstrates the technical feasibility of optical frequency domain imaging in peripheral interventions and identifies calcified nodules as a key risk factor for DCB failure.
score.bottom_line: OFDI-guided DCB angioplasty is feasible in selected femoropopliteal lesions, but the presence of an OFDI-detected calcified nodule significantly increases the risk of restenosis at 1 year.

title: First Experience of a New Transfemoral Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement System.

score.why_it_matters: Reports the initial procedural feasibility and early outcomes of a novel transfemoral transcatheter mitral valve replacement system.
score.bottom_line: This first-in-human experience demonstrates preliminary technical feasibility for a new transfemoral TMVR device, though broader clinical adoption awaits rigorous prospective trial evaluation.

title: Prehabilitation of Patients With Severe Tricuspid Regurgitation Before Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair.

score.bottom_line: Optimizing nutrition, decongestion, and physical status prior to tricuspid transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is emerging as an important strategy to reduce procedural risk in high-morbidity patients.

title: One-Lung Ventilation to Facilitate Transcatheter Tricuspid Edge-to-Edge Repair Under Transesophageal Echocardiographic Imaging.

score.why_it_matters: Proposes a specialized anesthetic maneuver to overcome challenging acoustic shadowing or lung interference during transesophageal echocardiography-guided tricuspid repair.
score.bottom_line: One-lung ventilation can be considered as a salvage or optimization technique to enhance TEE acoustic windows during transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair in anatomically difficult cases.

title: Pericoronary Inflammation With and Without Atherosclerosis: Marker, Mediator, or Both?

score.bottom_line: Assessment of pericoronary inflammation via coronary CTA provides mechanistic insight into residual inflammatory risk, but its direct therapeutic role in clinical practice remains investigational.

title: Impact of inflammation in patients with controlled standard modifiable risk factors (SMuRFs) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention.

score.why_it_matters: It assesses whether residual inflammatory risk drives adverse ischemic outcomes in PCI patients whose standard traditional risk factors are already optimized.
score.bottom_line: Even with optimal control of traditional risk factors (SMuRFs), persistent inflammation remains a key predictor of residual cardiovascular risk following PCI.

title: Acute heart failure in emergency settings.
abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) represents a major cause of emergency medical care worldwide and continues to carry a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality despite advances in chronic heart failure management. Most patients with AHF present to emergency departments (EDs), where the first hours of care are critical to determine prognosis. Of these, some have been previously evaluated and treated by prehospital emergency medical services before ED arrival. This consensus document summarizes the current evidence and provides practical advice to emergency physicians for the diagnosis, treatment, and disposition of patients with AHF in these emergency settings (emergency medical services and ED). It emphasizes the importance of a rapid phenotypic classification into acute decompensated heart failure, acute pulmonary oedema, isolated right ventricular failure, or cardiogenic shock, as a key tool to guide early management and triage decisions. It reviews evidence on prehospital and ED management, including the use of biomarkers, imaging, ventilatory support, diuretic and vasodilator strategies, and early initiation or continuation of guideline-directed medical therapy. It also discusses risk stratification and disposition decisions supported by validated tools. Finally, it identifies major knowledge gaps and future research priorities, including pragmatic trials to assess prehospital interventions, biomarker-guided therapy, and early initiation of disease-modifying treatments. Ultimately, this consensus document is aimed to contribute to the improvement of outcomes in AHF.

score.why_it_matters: Provides a practical, multidisciplinary consensus tailored to emergency and prehospital clinicians for the crucial first hours of acute heart failure management.
score.bottom_line: Prioritizes immediate bedside clinical phenotyping into four distinct profiles (decompensated HF, pulmonary edema, isolated RV failure, and cardiogenic shock) to guide early targeted therapies, rapid decongestion, and structured disposition.

title: Incidence, Modifiable Risk Factors, and Management of Cardiomyopathy After Ventricular Leadless Pacemaker Implantation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Leadless ventricular pacemakers (LPM) provide only RV pacing, which may lead to pacing-induced cardiomyopathy (PICM). It is unclear whether LPM implant site or atrioventricular synchronous pacing using the Micra AV device influence PICM occurrence.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the incidence of cardiomyopathy after LPM implantation and explore the association of implant site and AV-synchronous pacing with cardiomyopathy risk and LVEF evolution.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included 401 patients implanted with an LPM (Micra AV n=145) between July 2015 and March 2025. PICM was defined as cardiomyopathy (≥10% LVEF decline to <50%) in the presence of >20% ventricular pacing, where pacing was considered the primary cause. Risk factors for cardiomyopathy and LVEF evolution were assessed using Cox regression and mixed-effects modelling.
RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 33.0 months, all-cause cardiomyopathy occurred in 13.6% (4.8%/year), while PICM was identified in 5.5% (1.9%/year). RVOT implantation was independently associated with a lower incidence of all-cause cardiomyopathy (HR 0.48, P=0.019), and a slower LVEF decline (-0.56%/year vs -1.43%/year, P=0.013) compared with mid-septal implantation. Device type (Micra AV vs VR) was not associated with clinical outcomes or LVEF evolution. Among patients developing cardiomyopathy, 92.7% were medically treated, with 57.9% achieving ≥10% LVEF improvement, and 36.8% complete recovery. CRT upgrade was uncommon (7.3%).
CONCLUSION: Cardiomyopathy occurred in a substantial proportion of LPM recipients. RVOT implantation was associated with lower cardiomyopathy incidence and slower LVEF decline, whereas Micra AV implantation did not improve clinical outcomes. However, higher AV synchrony was linked to slower LVEF deterioration.

title: Endometrial ablation plus levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system versus endometrial ablation alone in women with heavy menstrual bleeding in The Netherlands (MIRA2): a multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endometrial ablation is an established and effective treatment for women with heavy menstrual bleeding, but many patients require further treatment, with approximately 10% ultimately undergoing a hysterectomy within 2 years. The insertion of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) immediately after endometrial ablation might inactivate residual untreated endometrium or prevent its regeneration, thereby preventing recurrent symptoms necessitating a hysterectomy. The aim of the study was to assess whether LNG-IUS insertion immediately after endometrial ablation in women with heavy menstrual bleeding reduced the need for subsequent hysterectomy within 2 years compared with endometrial ablation alone.
METHODS: This multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial was conducted in 34 hospitals in the Netherlands. Women younger than 60 years with heavy menstrual bleeding who were eligible for endometrial ablation were included and randomly assigned (1:1) to combined treatment comprising endometrial ablation plus LNG-IUS or to standard care comprising endometrial ablation alone (stratified by dysmenorrhoea and age). Masking was not applied. Endometrial ablation was done using electrical radiofrequency ablation or by transcervical resection of the endometrium. In participants allocated to combined treatment, intrauterine insertion of an LNG-IUS containing a total of 52 mg of levonorgestrel (releasing 20 μg per day in the first year) was done immediately after the ablative procedure. The primary outcome was the incidence of hysterectomy within 2 years, analysed on a modified intention-to-treat basis in all participants with available data. Serious adverse events were systematically assessed at 6 weeks, 12 months, and 24 months after the intervention. This study was registered on the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (NL-OMON54839) and is complete.
FINDINGS: Between Nov 19, 2019, and April 5, 2023, 715 participants were randomly assigned to combined treatment (n=359) or endometrial ablation alone (n=356). The median age of all participants was 45 years (IQR 40-48). 42 (6%) participants had missing data for the primary outcome at 2 years of follow-up. A hysterectomy was done in 15 (4%) of 342 participants in the combined treatment group versus 34 (10%) of 331 participants in the endometrial ablation group, corresponding to a relative risk (RR) of 0·43 (95% CI 0·24 to 0·77; p=0·0050), with a risk difference of -0·06 (95% CI -0·10 to -0·02; p=0·0040). Serious adverse events were reported in 27 (8%) of 346 participants in the combined treatment group and 26 (8%) of 327 participants in the endometrial ablation alone group (RR 0·98, 95% CI 0·59-1·65; p=0·94), and there were no treatment-related deaths.
INTERPRETATION: The combination of endometrial ablation and LNG-IUS significantly reduced the incidence of hysterectomy compared with endometrial ablation alone. The combined treatment appears to be a safe adjunctive strategy for heavy menstrual bleeding that does not increase the risk of complications.
FUNDING: The Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development.

title: Specific effects of Pulsed Field Ablation on the cardiac tissue, the nervous system and the conduction system in experimental and clinical studies.
abstract:
AIMS: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a novel ablation modality for the treatment of cardiac arrhythmias and has rapidly reshaped contemporary electrophysiology practice. This article provides a comprehensive analysis on the mechanisms underlying the specific effects of PFA on myocardial, neural tissue structures, and the cardiac conduction system, integrating biophysical principles with preclinical and clinical evidence relevant to contemporary electrophysiology practice.
METHODS AND RESULTS: This document provides an exhaustive mechanistic explanation for the preferential effects of PFA on myocardium and the limits of the 'tissue-selectivity' concept. The complex interplay between cellular and tissue-level biophysics, biological responses, and tissue regenerative capacity that determines differential susceptibility to electroporation across tissues is analysed. Distinct patterns of lesion formation and maturation following PFA are also reviewed, highlighting the temporal and histopathological differences compared with radiofrequency ablation. Additionally, lesion formation in heterogeneous substrates is analysed, including fibrotic and adipose-rich myocardium, where local electric field distribution critically influences lesion durability.
CONCLUSION: The article further examines the interaction between pulsed electric fields and neural tissue, with emphasis on the phrenic nerve and intrinsic cardiac autonomic nervous system. While nerve stimulation and transient reversible conduction disturbances produced by reversible electroporation can occur during ablation, permanent neural injury appears extremely rare in current clinical experience. Finally, this manuscript examines current understanding regarding the specific effects of PFA on the cardiac conduction system, which according to the limited available evidence appear strongly dependent on electric field dose and anatomical proximity.

score.why_it_matters: Provides a detailed mechanistic synthesis of pulsed field ablation biophysics, highlighting tissue selectivity boundaries and safety profiles concerning neural and conduction system structures.
score.bottom_line: While pulsed field ablation offers preferential myocardial injury with low rates of permanent neural damage, local electric field intensity and tissue heterogeneity remain critical determinants of lesion durability and conduction system safety.

title: Safety considerations and clinical monitoring during pulsed field ablation.
abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a transformative technology in cardiac electrophysiology, offering a potentially superior safety profile compared with thermal ablation due to its non-thermal mechanism of irreversible electroporation. Clinical experience confirms a substantial reduction in traditional complications such as pulmonary vein stenosis, atrio-oesophageal fistula, and permanent phrenic nerve injury, though PFA introduces a distinct spectrum of physiologic effects requiring consideration. Coronary vasospasm is the most characteristic phenomenon, ranging from transient, subclinical constriction to rare ischaemic or arrhythmic events; mitigation relies on coronary anatomical awareness, optimized lesion placement, and prophylactic vasodilators. Haemolysis, caused by red blood cell electroporation, varies with catheter design and pulse burden and is typically mild, though high exposure and inadequate hydration may rarely lead to acute kidney injury. Silent cerebral lesions could result from procedural and/or energy-related factors, including gas formation, air ingress, catheter manipulation, and anticoagulation management, with uncertain long-term clinical impact but opportunities for technique-driven reduction. Interactions between PFA and cardiac implantable electronic devices are system- and context-dependent, with monopolar configurations and catheter-lead proximity influencing the risk of transient interference and rare permanent damage.

score.why_it_matters: As pulsed field ablation enters widespread adoption, understanding its unique safety profile—including coronary vasospasm, hemolysis-induced kidney injury, and CIED interference—is critical for procedural safety.
score.bottom_line: While pulsed field ablation avoids thermal collateral damage, operators must remain vigilant for novel risks such as coronary vasospasm and hemolysis, requiring adequate hydration, prophylactic vasodilators, and careful CIED management.

title: Pulsed field ablation: from concepts to technology.
abstract:
AIMS: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a transformative approach for treating cardiac arrhythmias by exploiting irreversible electroporation to preferentially injure myocardium while limiting collateral damage. Translating this biophysical principle into safe and effective clinical systems requires careful integration of waveform design, catheter engineering, computational and experimental modelling, safety testing, and procedural workflow.
OBJECTIVE: This review summarizes the fundamental physical and engineering principles that govern cardiac PFA and examines how these principles influence efficacy, safety, lesion formation, and clinical usability.
BIOPHYSICAL AND TECHNICAL CONSIDERATIONS: Electroporation is governed primarily by the local electric field and waveform-dependent lethal thresholds rather than generator voltage alone. Key waveform variables include monophasic vs. biphasic pulses, microsecond vs. nanosecond pulse widths, duty cycle, and total application duration. Catheter design further determines electric field distribution, lesion geometry, current density, and applicability across anatomic targets, with important distinctions between bipolar and monopolar configurations.
MODELLING AND SAFETY: Experimental and computational approaches used to investigate PFA include finite element simulations, cell culture systems, vegetal substrates, and in vivo animal models, each with distinct strengths and limitations. High-voltage pulse delivery can also produce unintended effects, including Joule heating, electrochemical reactions, bubble formation, arcing, and interactions with implanted electronic devices. These phenomena highlight the importance of optimized waveform design, electrode configuration, and safety monitoring.
CLINICAL USABILITY: Clinical adoption depends not only on biological efficacy and safety but also on workflow efficiency, catheter versatility, procedure duration, mapping integration, anaesthesia requirements, and adaptability to differing clinical practices and geographic settings.
CONCLUSIONS: The performance of a PFA system reflects the interaction of biophysics, waveform characteristics, catheter design, modelling, safety controls, and procedural usability. Understanding these interconnected principles is essential for developing PFA technologies that are effective, safe, predictable, and practical for contemporary electrophysiology laboratories.

score.why_it_matters: Provides electrophysiologists with an in-depth understanding of the biophysical, engineering, and waveform characteristics that govern pulsed field ablation efficacy and potential safety hazards.
score.bottom_line: Pulsed field ablation outcomes depend fundamentally on local electric field thresholds, catheter geometry, and waveform parameters rather than raw generator voltage alone. Awareness of unintended effects such as microbubble formation and Joule heating is essential for optimizing clinical application.

title: Biophysical principles of pulsed field ablation.
abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is emerging as a major advance in cardiac ablation because it induces irreversible electroporation rather than relying primarily on thermal injury. This article provides an overview of the core biophysical principles underlying PFA, focusing on concepts broadly relevant across systems and clinical applications. Externally applied pulsed electric fields interact with biological tissues and affect their transmembrane potential. When a critical threshold is exceeded, nanoscale aqueous pores form in the lipid bilayer, initiating electroporation. Depending on pulse amplitude, duration, number, repetition frequency, waveform, and tissue characteristics, membrane permeabilization may remain reversible or progress to irreversible injury and cell death. This article focuses on the fundamental biophysical principles of electroporation that underpin PFA. The article outlines how membrane charging, cell geometry, and tissue heterogeneity influence electric field distribution and biological response and explains why lesion formation depends on both field intensity and exposure conditions. It also summarizes the molecular basis of pore formation, the potential contribution of lipid peroxidation and membrane proteins, and the downstream processes linking sustained permeability to loss of homeostasis and delayed cell death. Finally, it places cardiac PFA in the broader context of electroporation-based therapies developed in oncology, drug delivery, and gene transfer, while highlighting the remaining need for cardiomyocyte-specific mechanistic evidence to further optimize safety, precision, and durability.

score.why_it_matters: Understanding the biophysical mechanisms of pulsed field ablation provides electrophysiologists with crucial insights into how energy parameters and tissue properties influence lesion efficacy and safety.
score.bottom_line: This review outlines the biophysical principles of irreversible electroporation in cardiac tissue, detailing how waveform, field distribution, and cellular geometry determine lesion formation.

title: Treatment of paroxysmal and persistent atrial fibrillation with pulsed field ablation.
abstract: Pulsed field ablation has emerged as a novel energy source for atrial fibrillation ablation, offering preferential myocardial ablation with a favourable safety profile. Contemporary paroxysmal AF clinical studies demonstrate 12-month freedom from atrial arrhythmia recurrence in approximately 75-85% of patients, with major complication rates generally ranging from 1 to 3%. Compared with thermal ablation, PFA offers comparable efficacy and streamlined procedural workflows. In persistent AF, PVI remains the foundation of ablation, while additional adjunctive strategies are increasingly evaluated. Current evidence suggests that PFA can achieve 12-month arrhythmia-free outcomes generally ranging from approximately 60-75% in persistent AF populations. Major procedure-related complications typically occur in <3% of cases, supporting the feasibility of broader lesion sets with an acceptable safety profile. However, the incremental benefit of adjunctive ablation beyond PVI and the optimal lesion set for persistent AF remain to be assessed further Outcome assessment after PFA requires consideration of evolving endpoints. The clinical relevance of the traditional post-ablation blanking period is being re-evaluated, while continuous rhythm monitoring and AF burden are increasingly incorporated alongside conventional recurrence endpoints. Patient-reported outcomes are an important component of PFA evaluation. Compared with thermal ablation, PFA is associated with improved procedural tolerability, reduced analgesic requirements, rapid recovery, and the potential for same-day discharge. These features, together with favourable efficacy and safety outcomes, may contribute to broader adoption of PFA across both paroxysmal and persistent AF populations.

score.why_it_matters: Provides a comprehensive overview of safety, efficacy, and evolving clinical endpoints for pulsed field ablation in paroxysmal and persistent atrial fibrillation.
score.bottom_line: Pulsed field ablation demonstrates 12-month arrhythmia freedom of 75-85% in paroxysmal AF and 60-75% in persistent AF with major complication rates under 3%. It offers comparable efficacy to thermal ablation alongside streamlined procedural workflows and favorable recovery profiles.

title: Controlling pulsed field ablation efficacy during ablation procedures.
abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has rapidly emerged as a promising ablation modality for the treatment of cardiac arrhythmias because of its myocardial tissue preferential ablation and favourable safety profile. However, procedural control of lesion formation and reliable assessment of lesion durability remain important challenges. This review summarizes the main determinants of PFA efficacy and current approaches for intraprocedural lesion assessment. Experimental and clinical studies indicate that PFA lesion formation results from the interaction between delivered electrical energy, catheter design, tissue coupling, and application strategy. Lesion size and geometry are primarily determined by electric field distribution and cumulative electroporation exposure, while excessive energy delivery may induce unwanted thermal or electrochemical effects. Procedural efficacy also depends on stable catheter positioning, adequate tissue proximity, and sufficient lesion overlap. Unlike thermal ablation technologies, conventional procedural markers such as electrogram attenuation, impedance changes, and pacing threshold variation correlate poorly with durable irreversible electroporation. Multiparametric lesion estimation models integrating electrical, mechanical, and positional data have shown encouraging preclinical results, although clinical validation remains limited. Emerging strategies combining electroanatomical mapping, imaging, and automated electrogram analysis may improve real-time evaluation of lesion continuity and durability. Current PFA workflows rely mainly on standardized energy delivery protocols, optimized catheter positioning, and lesion overlap rather than real-time titration of energy. Although robust intraprocedural markers of irreversible electroporation are still lacking, ongoing advances in catheter technology, imaging, and lesion assessment tools are expected to improve procedural reproducibility and long-term lesion durability. Further studies are needed to establish validated endpoints for durable PFA lesion formation.

score.why_it_matters: As pulsed field ablation enters widespread adoption, understanding why conventional ablation endpoints fail and how contact and geometry drive lesion durability is critical for electrophysiologists.
score.bottom_line: Conventional procedural endpoints like impedance drop or electrogram attenuation correlate poorly with durable irreversible electroporation. Current PFA relies on standardized protocols and optimal tissue contact rather than real-time energy titration, highlighting the need for validated intraprocedural lesion markers.

title: Sedation and anaesthesia in pulsed-field ablation for atrial fibrillation: mechanisms, procedural requirements, and real-world practice.
abstract: Pulsed-field ablation (PFA) has rapidly emerged as an important energy source for atrial fibrillation ablation, offering tissue selectivity and procedural efficiency while introducing specific anaesthetic and sedation requirements. This narrative review examines the rationale for anaesthesia and sedation during PFA, the mechanisms underlying pain, involuntary movement, and neuromuscular stimulation, and the implications of catheter design, waveform characteristics, and patient-related factors for peri-procedural management. Available evidence indicates that both deep sedation and general anaesthesia can provide safe and effective procedural conditions when supported by appropriate monitoring, airway rescue capability, and experienced multidisciplinary teams. Deep sedation may offer advantages in workflow, recovery, and patient-centred care, particularly for standard pulmonary vein isolation procedures using contemporary biphasic systems with reduced muscle activation, whereas general anaesthesia remains appropriate for complex procedures, patients with substantial comorbidity, or settings in which complete immobility and airway control are essential. Current real-world practice is highly heterogeneous across regions and institutions, reflecting differences in regulations, staffing models, procedural complexity, and local expertise rather than a universally accepted standard. Overall, anaesthetic strategy in PFA should be individualised according to patient risk profile, expected procedural demands, and device-specific stimulation burden. Further prospective comparative studies are needed to define optimal sedation depth, standardise monitoring and outcome measures, and clarify how emerging technologies may enable lighter yet still effective sedation pathways.

score.why_it_matters: Provides a comprehensive overview of sedation strategies, pain mechanisms, and neuromuscular stimulation nuances unique to pulsed-field ablation in clinical electrophysiology.
score.bottom_line: Both deep sedation and general anaesthesia are effective for pulsed-field ablation, allowing centres to tailor their approach based on patient comorbidity, procedural complexity, and local staffing models.

title: The future of PFA in cardiac ablation procedures.
abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has rapidly emerged as a major development in catheter ablation, with increasing clinical adoption driven by procedural efficiency and a favorable safety profile compared with thermal energies. This article summarizes the future directions of PFA in electrophysiology, focusing on technological innovation, and how these advances are expected to expand PFA clinical indications. Additionally, this article provides a perspective on current gaps and future challenges of PFA. A perspective on future developments in new waveforms, catheter architectures, and integration with electroanatomical mapping systems for PFA is summarized. The document discusses novel waveform configurations and catheter design concepts that may improve lesion quality, procedural versatility, and safety. Additionally, this article also reviews how parallel advances in electroanatomical mapping integration, artificial intelligence, and robotic navigation are expected to enhance procedural guidance and enable individualized therapy. This manuscript summarizes the potential applications of PFA beyond pulmonary vein isolation and how emerging evidence supports its feasibility for linear atrial lesions, substrate modification, treatment of complex atrial tachycardias, and ventricular arrhythmia ablation. In addition, this article provides insights on how PFA may facilitate catheter ablation in new patient populations including elderly patients and those with higher procedural risks. Finally, this manuscript provides an outlook at major remaining challenges and knowledge gaps for PFA. The lack of homogenous procedural endpoints definitions and lesion durability assessment are discussed. Furthermore, this article highlights the need for standardized terminology and reporting in an environment where the high heterogeneity between available commercial systems complicates comparison across technologies.

score.why_it_matters: Provides a comprehensive overview of the next technological frontiers and clinical expansions for pulsed field ablation beyond simple pulmonary vein isolation.
score.bottom_line: While pulsed field ablation is rapidly being adopted for pulmonary vein isolation, future expansion into ventricular arrhythmias and substrate modification requires overcoming challenges in lesion durability, system heterogeneity, and standardized procedural endpoints.

title: The perspective of combining pulsed field ablation and left atrial appendage closure.
abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) and left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) are increasingly discussed as complementary strategies in atrial fibrillation (AF) care, addressing rhythm control and long-term thromboembolic risk. The rationale is attractive, but the current evidence base is uneven. Randomized evidence for LAAC around AF ablation is strongest for thermal-ablation-era workflows, particularly the OPTION trial, which showed lower non-procedure-related major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding with LAAC than with oral anticoagulation (OAC) and non-inferiority for death, stroke, or systemic embolism. Dedicated PFA-specific evidence remains limited to feasibility studies and early observational experience, and no trial has demonstrated that combined ablation-LAAC procedures are clinically superior when the ablation component is performed with PFA rather than radiofrequency or cryoballoon ablation. In parallel, OAC-withdrawal trials after apparently successful ablation, including OCEAN and ALONE-AF, have reported low thromboembolic event rates in selected lower-risk populations, whereas CLOSURE-AF cautions against simple extrapolation of LAAC benefit to older, frailer patients at high stroke and bleeding risk. This review therefore positions combined PFA-LAAC as a potential option for carefully selected patients rather than an established routine strategy. We summarize procedural workflow, patient selection, trial populations, device-platform considerations, reimbursement and organizational issues, and the main uncertainties that should guide future prospective studies.

score.why_it_matters: Provides a timely clinical perspective on combining pulsed field ablation with left atrial appendage closure in light of recent trial data.
score.bottom_line: Concomitant PFA and LAAC is technically feasible but lacks randomized outcome data; it should remain a tailored option for selected high-bleeding-risk patients rather than routine practice.
